  • Demising Walls, Exterior Walls, COM

docs.title: Ribbon Board
docs.text: The ribbon is let into the studs of a balloon wall and carries the joists. Rim sits at the joist ends, blocking between them: three different rows. Archived detail: "ribbon per standards" at the truss bottom chord and "2x flat ribbon" at the top chord. The ribbon size and location come from a detail like this; without it the row is not needed.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A ribbon (ribband, let-in ledger) is a horizontal board let into the studs that carries the joists or trusses in balloon framing and at top chord bearing. Do not confuse it with Rim (joist ends) and Blocking (between joists). A drywall ledger on a wall parallel to the joists is on the Bracing for Drywall page.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Wall section at the floor or roof whether there is a ribbon, let-in, size, FRT Truss bearing detail top chord bearing: blocking between the trusses instead of a ribbon Floor framing plan length of the walls the ribbon runs along

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Line (L) along the wall where the detail shows a ribbon, on the framing sheet with the F point. Takeoff framing/<floor> framing/details/ribbon or details/rb. Length = the length where the detail applies, not the leader length.

Line along where the detail applies: the line length goes to G of the DFL row, the detail name gives the M flag on export.

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text:
Export: the DT button; the name ribbon or rb gives the rb flag in M; the C_RimBoardBlockingHangers macro fills the Ribbon Board row.

Tree name A (Label) B (material) C D E details/ribbon Ribbon Board per detail: 2x4 at trusses, joist size (2x10) under joists =CEILING(G*1.1/D,1) 16 detail details/ribbon int Ribbon Board interior 16 details/ribbon + bd Ribbon Board interior + drywall 2x4 16 detail + drywall ledger

Factor 1.1 once in the formula, as for blocking and ledger: Formulas. Rule: top chord bearing trusses do not need a 2x4 ribbon. There you count blocking between the trusses, often (2) 2x6 over a 2x6 wall. The exterior ribbon is FRT if the exterior wall is FRT.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A ribbon added out of habit at top chord bearing trusses: blocking is needed.
  • Ribbon, rim and blocking written as one row or with mixed-up materials.
  • The trusses bear over the wall and the material is called ribbon, though the detail gives blocking or a drywall ledger.
  • Length taken from the detail leader, not from the walls where the detail applies.
  • All floor framing mistakes

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A B C D E Ribbon Board 2x4 =CEILING(G*1.1/D,1) 16 11/S400 Blocking (2) 2x6 =CEILING(G*2*1.1/D,1) 16 top chord bearing per 13/S400

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Rim Board, Blocking, Bracing for Drywall, Joist
  • Tips: Blocking

docs.title: Rim Board
docs.text: The rim board closes the joist ends around the floor perimeter and carries the wall above. It is counted in LFT along the perimeter, not in 16' boards. First floor framing: rim around the whole perimeter on the sill plate, the joist ends butt into it. Count LFT along the building perimeter and along the edges of floor openings; with I-joists the rim material is engineered only. Photo: hunker.com, source, found via Pinterest.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The rim is the board at the edge of the floor that the joist ends butt into: 1-1/8" OSB Rim, 1-1/4" LSL Rim, 1-3/4" LVL. With I-joists, engineered rim only. A Ribbon is let into the studs and carries the joists, Blocking sits between the joists: these are different rows. Rim around a deck or balcony is P.T. 2x in Deck / Porch / Balcony Frame.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Joist schedule, general notes rim product and thickness by joist depth Wall sections, floor details rim at the exterior wall, at demising on both sides, at roof TJI Deck / corridor details where the rim carries load and must be 1-3/4" LVL Floor framing plan perimeter and interior lines where the joist direction changes

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Line (L) along the rim line on the framing sheet with the F point: the outside perimeter of the floor plus interior lines where the joists change direction or butt into a wall. Line length = the length where the detail applies. Takeoff framing/<floor> framing/details/rim or with the detail number 5/S400 rim.

Line along where the detail applies: the line length goes to G of the DFL row, the detail name gives the M flag on export.

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text:
Export: the DT button puts details into J:L of the floor worksheet; a name with rim gets the r flag in M, and the C_RimBoardBlockingHangers macro moves the length to the Rim Board row.

Tree name A (Label) B (material) C D E details/rim Rim Board 11-7/8" Rim G x 1.05 (EWP) or G x 1.1 LFT detail details/rim LSL Rim Board 11-7/8" LSL Rim LFT details/rim corr LVL Rim Board 1-3/4 x 11-7/8 LVL LFT corridor detail details/rim dem Rim board dbl G x 2 LFT demising on both sides Product When 1-1/8" OSB Rim common thin rim per schedule 1-1/4" or 1-1/2" LSL Rim LSL is specified or a heavier rim is needed 1-3/4" LVL Rim a deck or corridor frame attaches to the rim, or the detail calls for it directly

Factor once in the formula: 1.05 on EWP jobs, 1.1 on all others (residential, COM, reconstruction). The canonical numbers: Formulas, same in Tips.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Rim called 1-3/4 LVL though LVL is not specified. Default is 11-7/8" Rim; product unclear - assumed in the note.
  • Rim split into 16' pieces. Keep LFT.
  • Rim at roof TJI forgotten.
  • At demising one side counted, the detail gives rim on both sides.
  • On a panel job the rim counted with the wall length, not along the floor line.
  • All floor framing mistakes

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A B C D E Rim Board 11-7/8" LSL Rim =CEILING(G*1.05,1) LFT 5/S400 Rim board dbl 11-7/8" LSL Rim =CEILING(G*2*1.05,1) LFT 9/S400 demising

docs.title: Screws
docs.text: Structural screws (SDS, SDWS, SDWC) per connection details: ledger to trusses, LVL packs, tie replacement. Counted in pcs by spacing or by the number per connection. P.T. deck ledger on a wall: hex-head structural screws in pairs at a spacing, a joist hanger at the top. Count screws in pieces per the ledger detail (number per point per spacing), with no washers or nuts. Photo: greenbuildingadvisor.com, source, found via Pinterest.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Screws are structural screws from the details: SDS 1/4 x 4 1/2, SDWS 22" ledger screw, SDWC (in lieu of H2.5A). They are counted only when the detail names them; we do not count nails. Screws need no washers or nuts. Bolts: Bolts.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Ledger details screw type, spacing or number per truss end (for example, 3 per end @ 16") Built-up beam, multi-ply LVL details SDS per pack, spacing and rows Roof-to-wall details 6" SDWC in lieu of H2.5A: either clips or screws, not both Stair detail screws for the stringer bottom bearing board

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text: Length from the detail Line (details/2x10 ledger + screws, details/12/S401), number of connections from the Count. No separate takeoff for screws is needed if they go with the ledger detail.

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text:
The screws row sits next to its connection. Formula in pcs: G - ledger LFT, H - spacing, multiplier - number of screws per connection, rounding significance = number per connection (3 per truss end gives ,3); round a result under 50 up to an even number.

A (Label) B C D E Screws 16" o.c. (3) SDWS 0.22 x 6" =CEILING(G*12/H*3*1.1,3) pcs ledger per 4/S401 Screws (2) SDS 1/4 x 4 1/2 connections x 2 pcs beam-to-post detail Screws SDWS 1/4 x 4 1/4 =4*4*G per stair pcs stair detail Screws 24" o.c. SDWC 6" by truss spacing pcs in lieu of H2.5A

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Ledger screws not per the detail: 1 per end instead of 3 (84 became 132).
  • Screws taken from another floor, not from their own ledger.
  • Details 1 and 3 look alike in the drawing, but the hardware is different.
  • Both H2.5A clips and SDWC counted when the detail says "in lieu of".
  • Nails counted in pieces.
  • All floor framing mistakes

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A B C D E G H Ledger 2x10 =CEILING(G*1.1/D,1) 16 4/S401 44 Screws 16" o.c. (3) SDWS 0.22 x 6" =CEILING(G*12/H*3*1.1,3) pcs 4/S401 44 16

docs.title: Steel Beam Web Fillers
docs.text: The steel beam is by others, but the wood nailer on the top flange, the filler in the web and their bolts are our rows. The top nailer sets the top-mount hanger for the joists. Basement: a steel W-beam on pipe columns carries wood joists. Steel and columns are by others; our rows are the nailer on the top flange, its bolts with washers and nuts, and hangers if the joists hang off the side. Photo: housedigest.com, source, found via Pinterest.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A nailer (nailer plate) is a board on the top flange of a steel beam that the joist hangers are nailed into; a web filler is a board in the beam web between the flanges for face-mount hangers or attachment. The steel itself (W12x26, HSS) is by others. We count the wood, bolts, washers, nuts and hangers.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take S framing plan lengths of the steel beams on this floor General framing notes typical note: double 2x plate bolted to top flange, 3/8" bolts staggered @ 24" o.c. Steel beam details (S4xx, S5xx) nailer on top and bottom, ripped to flange width, filler, hanger type Hanger schedule top-mount on the nailer or face-mount on the filler

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Line (L) along the steel beam centerline on the framing sheet with the F point: framing/<floor> framing/details/nailer or details/W12 nailer. Line length = beam length. Do not draw the steel as a Beam.

Line along where the detail applies: the line length goes to G of the DFL row, the detail name gives the M flag on export.

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text:
A block of four rows next to the beams of this floor. The nailer is double by default (note double 2x plate); single only if the detail clearly shows one layer. The bottom nailer under the flange and the filler are separate rows per the detail.

A (Label) B C D E Nailer Plates for Steel Beam (2) 2x8 (by flange width, 3x DF ripped) =CEILING(G*2/D,1) 16 14/S400 Anchor Bolts 24" o.c. (2) 3/8" Ø =CEILING(G*12/H*2*1.1,2) pcs note II.B Washers 24" o.c. (2) 3/8" Washers same formula pcs Nuts 24" o.c. (2) Nuts for 3/8" Ø same formula pcs Web Filler 2x6 =CEILING(G*2/D,1) 16 detail Hangers top-mount on the nailer, face-mount on the filler by joists pcs detail

The washer for a nailer bolt is a regular washer; 3x3 only if the detail calls for it.

docs.title: Nailer and packing by W profile
docs.text:
When the detail does not give the nailer size or the number of layers in the web, take them by the beam profile (W12x26: W12 series, weight 26 lb/ft). Packing (web filler) is the boards in the beam web, the number of layers for both sides together. The detail on the S sheet always wins over the table.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Nailer counted single without bolts, though the note gives double 2x with 3/8" bolts @ 24".
  • Bolts taken from the beams of another floor.
  • Face-mount hanger picked while the detail shows bearing on top of the nailer (top-mount), or the other way around.
  • Filler steel anchors with a 3x3 washer that is not specified.
  • EWP by others, and the LVL/LSL blocking at the steel beam per the detail not written.
  • All floor framing mistakes

(2) 3/8" Washers =CEILING(G*12/H*2*1.1,2) pcs 86 24 Nuts 24" o.c. (2) Nuts for 3/8" Ø =CEILING(G*12/H*2*1.1,2) pcs 86 24

docs.title: Canopy
docs.text: Archive 3D view: the canopy framing along the elevations is highlighted in red and lifted out. Its own joists or rafters, an edge beam, attachment to the wall and soffit underneath: a separate block, not part of the main roof. Entry canopy: a shed mini-roof on two timber brackets at the wall, soffit underneath, fascia at the edge. Count the canopy rafters or joists, the edge beam, brackets or posts, the wall attachment, soffit and fascia, all as a separate block. Photo: discoverydreamhomes.com, source, found via Pinterest.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A canopy is a small roof over an entry or along a facade: its own flat or sloped mini-roof, soffit underneath, attached to the wall with a ledger or a steel plate, sometimes on posts. It is a separate scope and a separate DFL worksheet, Canopy Framing List. A porch is bigger and usually on posts: Deck / Porch / Balcony Frame. A canopy is not part of the main roof eve and rake.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Elevations, roof plan (A) where the canopy is, dimensions, slope or flat Canopy details (A5xx, S5xx) beams, rafters or joists, spacing, wall attachment, posts RCP canopy soffit: material, layers, soffit framing Roof assembly notes canopy deck: 3/4" T&G OSB, tapered insulation, cover board Steel details steel plate and anchor bolts to the wall or column

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Part Tool Branch and name Canopy area (deck and soffit) Area (A) sqfts/canopy or sqfts/flat canopy Canopy joists or rafters J Area (J) framing/<floor> framing/joists/flat canopy 2x6 24" Canopy beams Beam (B) framing/<floor> framing/beams/FB30 12 Ledger to the wall Line (L) framing/<floor> framing/details/canopy ledger Posts Count (P) framing/<floor> framing/posts/6x6 P.T. 9

The floor is the one whose floor framing the canopy attaches to. The canopy has its own slope; a flat canopy has no slope factor.

J Area: outline, direction and spacing; the app figures the count and the lengths.

Canopy at the wall: ledger or steel plate with anchors, joists, edge beam, deck and soffit. The canopy is not part of eve/rake.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row
docs.text:
Export: the FR and JS buttons on the XL strip put the canopy takeoffs into Canopy Framing List; if the worksheet does not exist, it is created as a copy of the nearest floor. Block contents per detail:

A (Label) B C D E Beams (3) 2x10 points 12 FB30 Plates (2) with steel plate 2x10 LFT / 16 16 attachment detail Rafters 16" o.c. or Joists 24" o.c. 2x10, 2x6 from J Area lengths Hangers LUS210, HUC210-2 per connection pcs Anchor Bolts + Washers + Nuts 3/4" Ø x 5" per detail pcs steel plate to the wall Roof Sheathing at Canopy 3/4" T&G OSB SQ FT / 32 x 1.1 4x8 Tapered Insulation per spec SQ FT SQ FT Soffits at Canopy (2) 5/8" Glassmat or 5/8" Ext Gyp SQ FT x layers SQ FT RCP Frame 16" o.c. + Plate (2) 2x4 soffit framing LFT RCP

Framing not shown: a note right under the block header: Note: Canopy framing is not specified; all framing assumed; verify.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Canopy counted a second time in the main roof eve and rake.
  • Canopy soffit counted as regular gypsum when it needs exterior grade (5/8" Glassmat, DensGlass), two layers per detail.
  • Soffit area left out of the sheathing and WRB when the detail calls for it.
  • Canopy deck taken from the main roof spec when the detail calls for 3/4" T&G + tapered insulation.
  • Wall attachment (steel plate, anchor bolts, washers, nuts) missed.
  • Metal stud canopy joists counted as wood or not counted: follow the detail.
  • All roof mistakes

docs.title: Dbl / Trpl Rafters
docs.text: Archive 3D view: doubled rafters at the sides of an opening and under a load are highlighted in green. They run parallel to the regular rafters from the ridge to the wall and are counted like a beam with plies.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Dbl and Trpl Rafters are doubled or tripled rafters: at the sides of a roof opening (they carry the Roof Header), under a dormer wall, under an equipment load. Any size: 2x12, (2) 2x10, (3) 1 3/4 x 11 7/8 LVL. They bear on the Ridge, a wall or the floor framing. Regular rafters at a spacing are a J Area, see the Joist page.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof framing plan (S) where rafters are doubled or tripled, mark, size Sections, elevations sloped length from the ridge to the support; do not take the length from the plan Details bearing on a ridge beam (hangers) or on a ridge board (no hangers), ties to the wall Notes "every other rafter doubled": count from the plan, do not average

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Beam tool (B) along the rafter on the roof framing sheet with the F dot. One pack = one point with (n) in the name. The plan length is multiplied by the slope factor (6:12 gives 1.118, 8:12 gives 1.202; table on the Hip page) or taken from the section. The app rounds the order length (up to 8' to the foot, longer to an even number).

Hangers are needed only when the rafters bear on a bearing ridge beam or the detail shows them directly: LSSR, LRU by pack width. No hangers at a ridge board.

Beam tool: two points along the member, the app rounds the length and puts it into the takeoff name.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row
docs.text:
Path: framing/roof framing/beams/dbl rafters <size> <length>.

docs.title: Dormer
docs.text: Archive 3D view: dormers highlighted in red and lifted out. A gable dormer has a triangular gable and its own gable roof; a shed dormer has a flat single slope. Each has its own walls, roof, opening and trim. Shed dormer from the inside: front wall with windows, dormer rafters at a lower pitch, triangular side walls. All four parts are counted separately. Photo: HABS, Library of Congress, Public domain, source.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A dormer is a structure on a roof slope with its own roof and window. It combines four scopes: dormer walls, dormer roof, the opening in the main roof, trim. So a dormer does not hide in one item and does not dissolve into the main roof lines. Types: gable dormer (gable, two slopes, two valleys), shed dormer (one slope, below the ridge), eyebrow (rare, per detail).

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof plan (A), elevations number of dormers, type, dormer roof pitch, wall height Roof framing plan (S) header in the main roof, reinforced rafters at the sides, dormer rafters, valleys Sections through the dormer dormer wall height, rafter size, dormer ridge Window schedule dormer window Wall sections, details sheathing, WRB, FRT of dormer walls, dormer fascia and soffit

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore

docs.title: H-clips
docs.text: One clip per shared joint of two sheets between supports. Excerpt from the PSCL installation diagram: Simpson Strong-Tie, catalog C-C-2026, p. 340. We count joints, not edges. A row of H-clips on the free edge of the first roof sheathing sheet: one clip in each bay between rafters, the next sheet snaps into them. We count clips by sheet joints, not by edges. Photo: ggrhomeinspections.com, source, found via Pinterest.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
An H-clip (panel sheathing clip, PSCL) is a metal clip between the edges of two adjacent roof sheathing sheets. It keeps the free edges between rafters/trusses in one plane and sets the 1/8" gap. It is needed only on square edge panels; on T&G the tongue and groove hold the edge by themselves. Clip size = panel thickness (PSCL 19/32, PSCL 5/8).

Edge What it is Decision Square edge Straight edge, the sheets do not interlock Clips per detail and support spacing T&G (tongue and groove) The tongue fits into the neighbor's groove No clips, keep T&G in the material

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof sheathing notes (S) Thickness, span rating, edge type, PSCL @16" or edge support Truss layout / framing plan Support spacing in this particular zone: 24" o.c., 16" o.c.; each building has its own Roof details Solid blocking at joints (blocked diaphragm): a clip does not replace it

docs.title: How to count
docs.text:
1. Read the material, thickness, edge and support spacing of the zone. If both T&G and clips are specified, show the conflict in a Note; do not change the material.
  2. Count the shared joint of two sheets between adjacent supports: an 8' sheet at 24" o.c. gives 4 bays, at 16" o.c. 6 bays. Do not double it for the upper and lower sheet.
  3. Clips per sheet at 1 clip/span: 24" o.c. = 4, 16" o.c. = 6. For PSCA the manufacturer gives one clip up to a 28" span, two beyond that: do not carry 1 clip/span over to every roof.
  4. Clips = sheets x clips per sheet, waste added once after the calculation. For small slopes and offcuts the quantity is preliminary.
  5. Deck thicker than the spec threshold: no clips needed (check the panel table).

Sources: Simpson C-C-2026, p. 340, APA N335, sec. 3.6-3.7.

docs.title: DFL row
docs.text:
Source DFL row Material Unit Formula Roof Sheathing sheets Clips PSCL 19/32 (by thickness) pcs =sheets * clips per sheet T&G no row 3/4" T&G in the deck material

Note in the roof block: PSCL clips counted at 16" max per S203; 6 per 4x8 sheet allowed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Clips with a T&G deck.
  • Clips with a deck thicker than the threshold (23/32"): 11,000 extra pieces.
  • "4 per sheet" at 16" spacing (should be 6): 2540 instead of 3810.
  • 24" OWJ read as the support spacing, when it is the truss depth.
  • Spacing of one building carried over to another (storage 24", main 16").
  • Clip size not matched to the deck thickness.

All roof mistakes: common-mistakes.

Clips            PSCL 19/32         1240  pcs   206 x 6 (16" o.c.)

docs.title: Roof Header
docs.text: Archive 3D view: the roof opening header is highlighted in yellow, the reinforced rafters at the sides it bears on in green. The header length runs between those rafters.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A roof header is a horizontal beam in a sloped roof that frames an opening (skylight, chimney, dormer, hatch) or carries rafters within the slope. It bears on Dbl / Trpl Rafters or Posts. It is not a header over a window: window and door headers are on Headers.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof framing plan (S) roof openings, the header and the reinforced rafters next to it, mark Roof plan (A), RCP skylights, dormers, hatches and shafts through the roof Details, sections size, plies, hangers from header to rafters and from rafters to header Beam schedule size by mark

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Beam tool (B) between the reinforced rafters on the roof framing sheet with the F dot. One header = one point with (n) plies in the name; the app rounds the length (up to 8' to the foot, longer to an even number).

  1. Headers on both sides of the same opening (top and bottom of a skylight) are two points.
  2. The reinforced rafters at the sides are their own takeoff, see Dbl / Trpl Rafters.
  3. Hangers: header to rafters and cut rafters to header, by built-up width and skew/slope condition.

Beam tool: two points along the member, the app rounds the length and puts it into the takeoff name.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row
docs.text:

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Roof header counted a second time as a window header, or the other way around.
  • Header written, but the reinforced rafters at the sides and their hangers are missing.
  • Header size taken from another part of the roof; sizes change by zone.
  • Header in a panelized roof or in trusses by others counted as loose.
  • Hanger chosen without skew and slope on the pitch: ITS does not exist on a slope.
  • All roof mistakes

docs.text: A B C D E Header (2) 2x12 2 10 skylight per S201 Dbl Rafters 2x12 2 18 S201 Hangers LUS210-2 2 pcs 9/S501 Hangers LSSR210Z 6 pcs rafters to header The same connection up close: the header sits between two reinforced rafters, the cut rafters frame into the header on hangers. Dormer opening seen from the attic: doubled rafters at the edges and a header between them that the cut rafters frame into. Photo: Joe C. Freeman, HAER, Library of Congress, Public domain, source.

docs.title: Hip
docs.text: Archive 3D view: hip rafters highlighted in yellow, the outside edges where two slopes meet at a convex corner. At the top, the same roof in plan: the hip line on the plan is shorter than the real board.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A hip is the sloped outside edge where two slopes meet at a convex corner. The hip rafter runs from the wall corner to the ridge, it is longer and often deeper than a common rafter (2x12 with 2x10 rafters), and the jack rafters frame into it. The inside edge is a Valley; the top is the Ridge. On a truss roof the hip is built from hip trusses by others, and we count only the details around it.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof plan (A) where the hips are, pitch of the slopes on both sides Roof framing plan (S) hip rafter size, stick or trusses, mark Sections, elevations roof rise, sloped length Details hip bearing at the wall corner and at the ridge, hangers and ties

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Beam tool (B) along the hip line on the roof framing sheet with the F dot. The line on the plan is a horizontal projection; the real length is longer. Two ways:

  1. Take the sloped length from a section or elevation where the hip shows in true length.
  2. Multiply the plan length by the hip factor. For a hip at 45 degrees in plan (equal pitches on both sides): sqrt(1 + (pitch/12)^2 / 2).
Pitch Common rafter factor Hip and valley factor (45 degrees in plan) 4:12 1.054 1.027 6:12 1.118 1.061 8:12 1.202 1.106 10:12 1.302 1.161 12:12 1.414 1.225

Different pitches on the two sides of a hip: only from the section. The app rounds the result to an order length (up to 8' to the foot, longer to an even number).

Beam tool: two points along the member, the app rounds the length and puts it into the takeoff name.

The plan length is multiplied by the slope factor: that gives the board length. With different slope pitches take the length from the section.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Hip counted on a truss roof: there the hip trusses are by others.
  • Length taken from the plan without a factor, or with the common rafter factor (1.118 instead of 1.061).
  • Jack rafters at the hip not counted separately, or counted as full common rafters.
  • Hip and valley mixed up: outside corner and inside corner.
  • Engineered hip beam written without the product and plies.
  • All roof mistakes

docs.title: Overframes
docs.text: Archive 3D view: overframes highlighted in red, roof areas built on top of the lower roof. Under them runs the main roof deck, on top are their own rafters on sleepers. Section: the lower roof with its deck, 2x6 sleepers (valley plates) laid flat on it, the overframe rafters and their deck on top. Sleepers, rafters and the upper deck are our rows; the lower deck under the overframe per detail.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: An overframe (California framing, framed-over roof) is roof framing built on top of an already sheathed lower roof: the rafters bear on 2x6 sleepers (valley plates) laid flat on the lower deck. Piggyback trusses are built the same way: the upper part of a tall truss sits on sleepers over the lower one. A lot of material hides in the details, not on the plan.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof plan (A) overframe outline, pitch, where it lands on the lower roof Roof framing plan (S) stick overframe or piggyback trusses, rafter size, spacing Details, sections sleepers (2x6 flat, 2x6 bearing plates 4' o.c.), overframe ridge, deck under the overframe Truss notes piggyback: 2x6 sleepers and their spacing, cover board

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Part Tool Branch and name Overframe area Area (A) sqfts/overframe <pitch> (overframe 4), its own pitch Overframe rafters J Area (J) framing/roof framing/joists/overframe 2x8 24" Sleepers Line (L) along the lines where the rafters bear on the lower roof framing/roof framing/details/sleepers Overframe ridge Beam (B) framing/roof framing/beams/ridge ...

The overframe 4 area is counted separately from rf 6 and goes into roof sheathing with its own slope factor (once). An overframe is never added automatically: its area and materials come only from this building's plans.

Area along the zone outline: the area goes into sqfts and from there into the sheet count.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row

Takeoff name A (Label) B C D E sqfts/overframe 4 Roof Sheathing (overframes) per roof spec SQ FT x slope / 32 x 1.1 4x8 sheet details/sleepers Sleepers 2x6 =CEILING(G/D,1) 16 detail joists/overframe 2x8 24" Rafters 24" o.c. 2x8 from J Area lengths piggyback Sleepers or Bearing Plates 2x6 per detail per truss detail: spacing (often 4' o.c.) over the area of the upper trusses 16 truss detail

Piggyback is one assembly with two write-ups of the same thing: in Tips it is written as 2x6 sleepers, in COM as 2x6 bearing plates 4' o.c.. Count it per the current building's truss detail on one row, not two.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Overframe added "out of habit", or not added although the roof plan shows an addition over a slope.
  • Overframe pitch taken from the main roof.
  • Sleepers forgotten (about 400 2x6 boards at 16' on a big multifamily building).
  • Lower roof deck under the overframe subtracted or counted twice without a detail.
  • Cover board and layers over the overframe missed.
  • All roof mistakes

docs.title: Ridge
docs.text: Archive 3D view: the ridges of all roof parts highlighted in red and lifted out by run. Each run has its own length from the outside face of the exterior wall to the intersection with another ridge or hip.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The ridge is the top horizontal member of a sloped roof that the rafters frame into: a ridge board (2x12, the rafters work in pairs) or a ridge beam ((2) 1 3/4 x 11 7/8 LVL, carries the rafters and bears on Posts or gable walls). It is counted only on a stick-framed roof; with trusses the ridge is inside the truss, by others. The sloped edges are the Hip and Valley; the beam between reinforced rafters is the Roof Header.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof framing plan (S) ridge line, mark (RB1), size, plies, where the supports are Roof plan (A) ridge runs by roof part, where the ridge ends at a hip Sections, details ridge board or ridge beam, rafter hangers to the ridge beam, sub fascia Beam schedule size and material by mark

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Beam tool (B) along the ridge line on the roof framing sheet with the F dot. Length runs from the outside face of the exterior wall (not the inside face of the framing) to the end of the run. The app rounds the length: up to 8', up to the next foot; longer, to an even number.

  1. One ridge run = one point; a built-up ridge beam is one point with (2) in the name.
  2. A ridge beam needs posts or walls under its ends: the posts are counted in roof framing/posts.
  3. Rafters hang from the ridge beam on hangers (LSSR, LRU) per detail; no hangers at a ridge board.
  4. Sub fascia and ridge beam per detail are separate rows, even when the rafters are by others.

Beam tool: two points along the member, the app rounds the length and puts it into the takeoff name.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row

  • Length taken from the inside face of the wall or along a short line on the plan instead of to the outside face.
  • Ridge beam without posts and without the rafter hangers from the detail.
  • Several ridges at different heights written as one length.
  • Rim and blocking at roof TJI forgotten: a TJI roof is counted like floor framing.
  • All roof mistakes

docs.title: Roof Sheathing
docs.text: Plywood sheets on a slope: area = plan projection x slope factor, sheets = area / 32 x 1.1. Joints between supports are where H-clips go with square edge. Photo: Marshmallow, CC BY 2.0, source.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Roof sheathing is the deck over the trusses or rafters: OSB or plywood on the slopes, 3/4" on flat areas, ply under metal, a second layer at canopies. Each roof type has its own product and its own area (Roof Types). The soffit underneath is not deck. Together with the deck, the DFL gets the eave framing: sub fascia, blocking at eves, truss bracing, ties.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Structural roof framing plan, notes (s2xx rf) Product and thickness (roof table WRS-1 is separate from the wall table WS-1), span rating, fastening Arch roof plan (a105 rf) Slope outlines, pitches 6:12, overframes, flat zones Roof sections, details (sec, d) T&G or square edge, clips, blocking, sub fascia, heel, flat roof layers Truss package / layout Truss spacing (24" o.c.), piggyback and sleepers, bracing Roof assemblies (ft) Flat: cover board (Densdeck, glass mat), rigid, tapered, XPS, EPDM

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
1. The area comes from the sqfts branch: plan projection Area for each pitch and material: rf 6, rf mtl 4, overframe 4, flat, ply flat, flat grge (Roof SQFT). Garage, porch, storage have their own outlines and their own pitches.
  2. Take the pitch from this building's sheet. The factor sqrt(1+(rise/12)^2) is applied once, in the Excel formula; the name rf 6 does not change the geometry.
  3. The spec lives in the template cells R3 main, R4 overframes, R5 metal, R6 flat, R7 shingles; S holds a bare sheet reference (S203, 2/S500).
  4. Arch vs structural conflict: a main Note with both sources and the value used, for example Note: Roof sheathing differ, 19/32" per S612, 15/32" per A4-03; counted 19/32"; verify.
  5. H-clips are counted separately by edge type, thickness and support spacing: H-clips. No clips with T&G.

LFT

docs.text:
• Pitch not taken from the sheet, or applied twice (6:12 instead of 4:12 gave +3 sheets and +12 clips on a garage).
  • Clips with T&G or with a deck thicker than the threshold; "4 per sheet" instead of by support spacing.
  • 24" OWJ read as the spacing, when it is the truss depth.
  • On a flat roof, Densdeck / cover board and the second XPS layer missed.
  • Piggyback sleepers and 1x3 strapping under the trusses missed.
  • Ties not along all bearing lines; tie spacing not equal to truss spacing.
  • Soffit underneath counted as deck area.

docs.title: Valley
docs.text: Archive 3D view: valley rafters highlighted in green, the inside edges where two slopes meet at a concave corner. At the top, the roof in plan: the valley runs from the inside corner of the walls to the ridge. The valley rafter runs diagonally from the corner to the ridge, jack rafters frame into it from both sides. Photo: HABS, Library of Congress, Public domain, source.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: A valley is the sloped inside edge where two slopes meet at a concave corner (an addition, an L-shaped plan, a dormer). The valley rafter carries the jack rafters of both slopes, so it is deeper than a common rafter. The outside edge is a Hip. With an overframe, sleepers on the lower roof replace the valley rafter: Overframes. On a truss roof the valley is a set of valley trusses by others.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof plan (A) valley lines, slope pitches, where a dormer or addition is Roof framing plan (S) stick valley rafter or overframe, size, mark Sections rise, sloped length, bearing at the bottom of the valley Details jack rafter hangers to the valley, ice and water in the valley (not our scope unless specified)

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
Beam tool (B) along the valley line on the roof framing sheet with the F dot. The plan length is shorter than the real one: multiply by the factor from the table on the Hip page (for 45 degrees in plan: 6:12 gives 1.061, 8:12 gives 1.106) or take the length from the section. The app rounds to an order length.

  1. One valley = one point; a double valley (dormer on a large slope) gets (2) in the name.
  2. A valley at an overframe is not drawn as a rafter: there it is a Line along the sleepers.
  3. Lower roof sheathing under an addition: per detail, do not subtract or duplicate it automatically.

Beam tool: two points along the member, the app rounds the length and puts it into the takeoff name.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row
docs.text:
Path: framing/roof framing/beams/valley <size> <length>. The template's combined row Ridge / Valley / Hip in LFT when the job does not split them.

Takeoff name A (Label) B C D E beams/valley 2x12 16 Valley Rafters 2x12 points 16 S201 beams/valley (2) 2x12 14 Valley Rafters (2) 2x12 points 14 dormer details/sleepers Sleepers 2x6 LFT / 16 16 overframe

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Valley counted as a rafter on a truss roof or at an overframe.
  • Length taken from the plan without a factor.
  • Jack rafters of both slopes at the valley not accounted for.
  • Valley and hip mixed up.
  • Valley flashing added with no scope: Flashing.
  • All roof mistakes

docs.text: A B C D E Valley Rafters 2x12 2 16 S201, pitch 8:12 Rafters 16" o.c. 2x10 18 12 jack rafters at valley

docs.title: Base
docs.text: Wood baseboard along the bottom of the wall runs into the door casing: base is counted in LFT along the room perimeter, the door opening is deducted from the perimeter, casing is its own row. Photo: nadinestay.com, source, found via Pinterest. There is no baseboard behind kitchen cabinets: deduct the wall runs under the cabinets from the perimeter.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Baseboard: the board along the bottom of the wall in finished rooms. Counted in LFT along the room perimeter. Wood base only where the room schedule says Wd or Wood; tile, rubber, vinyl and metal base are a different material. Crown runs along the same perimeter, but with its own exclusions: Crown.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Room finish schedule Base column: material per room, TBD, unfinished rooms Floor plans Room perimeter, kitchen cabinets, stairs, garage Interior elevations, finish notes Exclusions and material when the schedule is silent

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text: Line along the room perimeter on the plan with the W point, continuous from the entry door, breaks only on purpose. One item per floor and zone: baseboard 1st, baseboard corridor. Unit base separately from corridors, lobby and other common areas, because they may have a different material. Bathrooms with tile base can be traced as a separate item to check the exclusion.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Rule What to check No base behind kitchen cabinets Deduct the walls under the cabinets in the formula Base under windows stays Do not skip the short runs under windows Stair junction Stop the base where the stair trim makes it unnecessary Toilets and shower rooms Count if the material is wood; do not count tile base as wood Garage, mechanical, crawl space, unfinished No base, do not run the perimeter through them Material TBD Base Leave the note Base not specified in room schedule instead of picking a product

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text:
Tree name DFL row Unit Formula trims/baseboard 1st Baseboard LFT =42+38+27+... all measured runs visible trims/baseboard corridor Baseboard corridor LFT separate from units Base material TBD LFT note, if the schedule does not set it

Every measured value goes into the formula: the checker must see where the number came from, not just the total.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Perimeter run through the kitchen cabinets and garage.
  • Tile base counted as wood base.
  • Units and corridors in one row with different materials.
  • Total as a number without the addends.
  • All Excel mistakes: Excel DFL and notes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Takeoffs/Main/trims/baseboard 1st   Line   412 LFT (7 rooms)

Baseboard   Wd 1x6 (per schedule)   412  LFT   =58+44+71+39+66+52+82   A701
Baseboard   TBD                     0    LFT   Note: Base not specified in room schedule
Show 5 archived cards with illustrations Base below windows Runs under windows stay unless the notes exclude them. Stair / wall junction Base stops where the stair trim makes it unnecessary. Toilets / shower rooms Check the material before excluding: wood is counted, tile is not. Garage and unfinished rooms No base in garage, mechanical, crawl space, unfinished storage. Excel formula All measured runs are visible in the formula; the total matches the material note.

docs.text:
• Interior Trims, Room Schedule, Crown, Casing

docs.title: Casing
docs.text: Window from the inside: head casing, side casing, stool, apron; door: head and two sides. Casing is counted in LFT with a formula from the opening list.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The trim around a door or window on the inside. Counted in LFT: the perimeter of one opening multiplied by the number of such openings. The list of doors and cased openings, size designations and Excel entry are on the Door and Window Trim page; this page has the casing and jamb formula.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Door schedule Size, type, number of doors; usually no trim type there Window schedule and interior elevations Windows with casing, stool and apron Finish schedule and notes Casing profile (1" x 3-1/2" Polyurethane casing), stained or painted

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text: No separate measurement is needed: casing is calculated with a formula from the list of doors and windows per floor. The door list comes from the plan (open door symbol) or the door schedule, windows from openings. Odd-shaped casing (arched, a cased opening across the whole wall) can be traced with a Line.

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text:
DFL row Unit Formula Casing for Int. Doors LFT =(2*H+W)*qty for each door size, both sides of the opening Casing for Ext. Doors&Wind LFT perimeter of 3 or 4 sides (with stool and apron) x quantity Int. Door jambs LFT = casing / 2, if the template counts jambs through casing Cased Openings casing LFT separate from doors
  • Group casing by location and type when common areas differ from units.
  • Keep the profile from the notes in the row or a note (Note: All door trim to be 1" x 3-1/2" Polyurethane casing); hardware numbers are not part of trim.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Casing counted on one side of the door instead of two.
  • Interior casing mixed with exterior casing and flashing.
  • A made-up profile instead of not specified.
  • All Excel mistakes: Excel DFL and notes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Int. Doors 2680                     24  pcs
Casing for Int. Doors   1x3-1/2     1008 LFT   =(2*8+2.5)*2*24
Int. Door jambs                     504  LFT   =C<casing>/2

docs.text:

  • Exterior Trims - Casing, Corner & Band

docs.title: Crown
docs.text: Crown molding around the ceiling perimeter. Counted in LFT in the same rooms as base, but with its own exclusions. Photo: The Finishing Company Richmond Va, CC BY 2.0, source

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Crowns: the molding at the wall-to-ceiling joint. Counted in LFT along the room perimeter, with the same logic as Base, but crown must not be derived from base: it has its own room list. It is included when the interior trim scope is active and crown is shown in the schedule or notes.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Room finish schedule, remarks Which rooms get crown, material, TBD RCP and ceiling notes Sloped ceiling, tray ceiling, height Interior elevations Crown profile, where it is shown

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text: Line along the perimeter of rooms with crown on the plan with the W point, one item per floor (crown 1st, crown 2nd). Second floor separately: crown there is often only in the hall, foyer and large bedrooms.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Rule What to check No crown in closets Exclude Closet / CLO. unless the scope says otherwise Sloped ceiling: no crown Watch for slope ceiling on the RCP Garage, mechanical, crawl space, unfinished: no crown Do not run the perimeter through them Bathrooms may have crown Do not exclude automatically, check the scope Second level Only the hall, foyer and large rooms where shown Material TBD Crowns Leave the note, do not pick a product

Do not confuse crown with exterior cornice, fascia, frieze and rake trim.

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text: Tree name DFL row Unit Formula trims/crown 1st Crowns LFT =58+44+71+... all runs visible trims/crown 2nd Crowns 2nd floor LFT as a separate row Crowns TBD LFT note, if the material is not set

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Crown counted in closets and rooms with a sloped ceiling.
  • Crown derived from base without its own room list.
  • Second floor counted in full.
  • All Excel mistakes: Excel DFL and notes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Takeoffs/Main/trims/crown 1st   Line   286 LFT (living, dining, foyer, hall)

Crowns   3-1/2" crown (per schedule)   286  LFT   =92+68+44+82   A701
Crowns   TBD                           0    LFT   Note: Crown material not specified; verify
Show 3 archived cards with illustrations No Crowns in closets Do not run the crown perimeter through closet walls. Sloped ceiling Check the RCP before counting: a sloped ceiling breaks the usual rule. Second level Only the hall, foyer and large rooms where it is required.

• Interior Trims, Base, Room Schedule, Casing

docs.title: Door and Window Trim
docs.text: Baseboard and door casing on one wall: base is counted by perimeter, casing with a formula from the door list. Photo: gemteck1, CC BY 2.0, source

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The list of interior doors and cased openings per floor, with size and type designation, from which the casing is calculated with a formula. The door schedule wins over the plan: if there is one, fill from it. The casing and jamb formula is on the Casing page; interior window trim (casing, stool, apron) only when it is in the finish schedule or details.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Door schedule (dr sch) Size, type (pocket, slider, bi-fold), material, F.R., S.C. Floor plans Open door symbol (count by it, not by the wall), cased openings C.O. Finish schedule, interior elevations Window casing, stool, apron; trim profile Notes Manufacturer or special product: keep it in the note, do not reduce it to a size

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text: Doors are counted with Count points on the open door symbol, one item per size and type (2680, (2)2680, 4080 C.O.), separately for each floor. Shower glass doors are not included. Mark unit entry doors with a fire rating in the name (2680 F.R.); hardware numbers are not needed.

docs.title: Size designations
docs.text:
Example Meaning How to write it 2680 2'-6" x 8'-0" regular single interior door (2)2680 two doors 2'-6" x 8'-0" double door, pair marker visible 2680 Pocket pocket door the word Pocket stays (2)3080 Slider two panels 3'-0" x 8'-0" quantity and Slider stay (2)2680 Bi-Fold closet bi-fold Bi-Fold, do not reduce it to slider 9068 Bi-Fold wide bi-fold 9'-0" x 8'-0" one opening, panels are not counted separately 2680 Metal F.R. S.C. metal, fire-rated, self-closing garage and mechanical; F.R. and S.C. stay 4080 C.O. cased opening 4'-0" x 8'-0" enter as a cased opening, not as a door

F.R. on a door means fire-rated (door, frame and hardware as an assembly). Do not confuse it with FRT: that is fire-retardant-treated framing lumber.

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text:
Tree name DFL row Unit Rule openings/1/2680 Int. Doors 2680 pcs per floor, from the schedule openings/1/(2)2680 Int. Doors (2)2680 pcs double as a pair openings/1/4080 C.O. Cased Openings 4080 pcs separate from doors Casing for Int. Doors LFT formula from the list, see Casing Interior Doors&Trims block header with a note about the profile

Excel entry:

  1. All doors and cased openings are entered per floor before the casing formulas.
  2. Sizes are rewritten in inches in a helper table: 2'-0" x 6'-8" becomes 24 x 80.
  3. Mark and quantity are copied to the helper table on the right; the casing formulas come from it; repeated doors are counted with a formula, not typed by hand.
  4. Before output, select the quantity cells and compare the sum in the status bar with the number of doors on the plans.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Doors counted by the wall or by a nearby note, not by the door symbol.
  • Bi-fold panels counted as separate doors.
  • Shower glass doors entered as interior doors.
  • Pocket, Slider, F.R. S.C. lost on the way to Excel.
  • A cased opening entered as a door.
  • All Excel mistakes: Excel DFL and notes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Takeoffs/Main/openings/1/2680          Count   18
Takeoffs/Main/openings/1/(2)2680       Count   3
Takeoffs/Main/openings/1/4080 C.O.     Count   2

Int. Doors 2680              18  pcs   A601
Int. Doors (2)2680           3   pcs   A601
Int. Doors 2680 Pocket       2   pcs   A601
Cased Openings 4080          2   pcs   A601
Casing for Int. Doors        1x3-1/2   ...  LFT   =(2*8+2.5)*2*18+...
Show 8 archived cards with illustrations Count by the open door symbol Count the actual swing, not a note by the wall. Size notation 2680 2680 = 2'-6" x 8'-0". Keep the designation the same all the way to Excel. Double doors Write (2)2680, pair marker visible. Pocket and Slider 2680 Pocket, (2)3080 Slider: the type stays in the designation. Shower glass doors Do not enter them as interior doors: that is shower scope. Cased opening C.O. is an opening with no door, entered separately. Entry per floor and helper table Doors and C.O. per floor; mark and quantity in the helper table for the casing formulas. There is a door schedule Fill from the schedule first, the plan comes second.

docs.text:

  • Windows and Doors, Standard notes

docs.title: Interior Trims
docs.text:
Interior Trims is a separate scope: baseboard, door and window casing, crown. Not exterior trims, not drywall and not framing. This section is needed when the job includes finish trim per the room schedule, door schedule or finish plans. In a frame scope interior trim is not counted.

Baseboard and crown are LFT along the room perimeter. Breaks (kitchen cabinets, garage, stair) must be intentional and visible in the formula.

docs.title: What is included and in what order
docs.text:
• Room Schedule

    How to read the room finish schedule: the Base column, Wd or tile material, unfinished rooms.

    Room Schedule

  • Base

    Baseboard along the room perimeter: where it goes and where it does not (kitchen cabinets, garage, tile base).

    Base

  • Crown

    Crown along the perimeter: no closets, sloped ceilings, garage.

    Crown

  • Door and Window Trim

    The list of doors and cased openings per floor, designations 2680, C.O., F.R. S.C., Excel entry.

    Door and Window Trim

  • Casing

    Interior door and window casing: formula from the opening list, jamb.

    Casing

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Prepare the sheets: floor plans, room finish schedule, door schedule, interior elevations. In OurPlanCore these are the fin and in el sheets in the units folder, plans with the W point.
  2. Read the room schedule: which base (Wd, tile, rubber, TBD), where crown goes, which rooms are unfinished.
  3. Trace the perimeters with a Line: Baseboard and Crowns continuous from the entry door, with intentional breaks. Unit base separately from corridors and lobby.
  4. Make the list of doors and cased openings per floor, then the casing with a formula from the list.
  5. Trim not specified: write not specified, do not guess the product.

docs.title: Key rules
docs.text:
• Garage, mechanical, crawl space, unfinished storage: no Baseboard and no Crowns.
  • Exclude tile base when the takeoff is for wood base.
  • Common areas (corridors, lobbies) separately from units: different trim.
  • Crowns are counted when the trim scope is active and crown is shown.
  • Door casing is filled in after the interior door list; casing of exterior doors and windows after the exterior openings.

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text: Tree name DFL row Unit Rule trims/baseboard 1st Baseboard LFT perimeter of finished rooms, formula with visible addends trims/crown 1st Crowns LFT only rooms with crown per the schedule openings list Int. Doors, Cased Openings pcs per floor, with the size designation Casing for Int. Doors LFT formula from the door list

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Base run through kitchen cabinets and the garage.
  • Crown counted in closets and rooms with a sloped ceiling.
  • Tile base counted as wood base.
  • Doors counted by the wall, not by the open door symbol.
  • All Excel mistakes: Excel DFL and notes.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Room Schedule, Base, Crown, Door and Window Trim, Casing
  • Exterior Trims, Windows and Doors
  • Standard notes, Takeoff item labels

docs.title: Room Schedule
docs.text: Room finish schedule columns: Floor, Base, Walls, Ceiling, Remarks. Wood base only with Wd; exclude tile base; the garage has no base and no crown.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The room finish schedule is the table on the fin sheets (or A6xx, A7xx): for each room, the floor, base, wall and ceiling material plus remarks. It tells you where to count Base and Crown and in what material. The door schedule (dr sch) gives the door list for Door and Window Trim.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Room finish schedule (fin) Base column: Wd, Tile, Rubber, TBD; Remarks column: crown, wainscot Door schedule (dr sch) Door size, type, fire rating Finish plans and interior elevations (in el) Where the finish is shown graphically Notes for common areas Corridors, lobby, bathrooms, units: differences

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
1. Find the Base column and go by it, not by the room name: a bathroom may have wood base and a kitchen tile.
  2. List the unfinished rooms (garage, mechanical, storage): they get neither base nor crown.
  3. Check Remarks and the ceiling notes: crown, sloped ceiling, tray ceiling.
  4. Material TBD or blank: the note Note: Base not specified in room schedule, do not pick a product.
  5. Count common areas and units with different materials in separate rows.

docs.title: Questions before counting
docs.text:
• Bathrooms with tile base or wood?
  • Corridors and lobbies: a different base or casing?
  • Crown everywhere, only in common areas, or in specific rooms?
  • Are door and window trims specified or not?

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Base taken by the room name, not by the Base column.
  • Unfinished rooms included in the perimeter.
  • TBD replaced with a made-up product.
  • All Excel mistakes: Excel DFL and notes.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • Interior Trims, Base, Crown, Casing, Door and Window Trim

docs.title: Eve / Eave
docs.text: Roof corner at the framing stage: on the left the sloped rake edge along the gable, on the right the horizontal eave with blocking between the truss tails. Eave and rake are different lines and different takeoffs. Photo: ssukotash, CC BY 2.0, source.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The eave (eve in the tree) is the lower horizontal edge of the roof along the wall, an overhang with soffit underneath and fascia on the end. The rake is the sloped edge on the gable (Rake), a return is the box at the corner where the eave turns into the rake (Returns). The vertical strip at the truss heel above the wall is Truss Heel, not part of the eave. From one eave line the export gets the soffit (SQ FT), fascia and sub fascia (LFT) and the overhang framing.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof plan (a105 rf) Eave lines around the perimeter, overhang, main vs porch and canopy Sections, soffit detail (sec, d) Overhang width, sub fascia 2x6/2x8, frame for soffit 2x4/2x6, soffit material Elevations (el) Fascia, frieze, material changes by elevation RCP Soffit under canopy and porch (its own branch, not eave) Finish schedule / specs Vinyl vented, beadboard, fiber cement, exterior gypsum

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
1. Line tool along the outer edge of the eave on the roof plan. LFT unit. All runs: every side of the building, every bump-out.
  2. Name: eve <overhang in inches> <zone>: eve 24 main, eve 12 porch, eve 18 upperporch no frame. Take the overhang from a section or detail, not from the line weight on the plan. The eves rakes/eves folder is created from the name automatically; do not change eves to eaves.
  3. Different overhangs and zones = different takeoffs. Mark runs with no overhang framing in the name (no frame).
  4. Canopy and porch are not part of the eave: they have their own takeoffs and their own block. The main mistake is counting them twice.
  5. Soffit SQ FT = length x width only when the width is constant. A complex porte-cochere or porch soffit is traced separately with an Area, without counting it a second time by length.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row
docs.text:
Takeoff name DFL row Material Unit Formula eves rakes/eves/eve 24 main Soffits at Eves 12" Vinyl vented / beadboard / 5/8" Ext Gyp SQ FT or LFT LFT x 24/12 same line Fascia at Eves 1x8 / alum wrapped LFT LFT x 1.1 same line Sub Fascia 2x8 LFT in the roof block same line Frame for Soffits 24" o.c. 2x4 or 2x6 per detail LFT per detail same line Blocking at Eves, Simpson Ties at Eves 2x6, H2.5A LFT, pcs Roof Sheathing eves rakes/eves/eve 12 porch the same rows in the porch block per porch detail separate from main

Excel export: XL strip, E/R button; the macro reads the overhang number in the name as the width in inches. Vinyl soffit is entered as a material in SQ FT, not as a framing row. If 30% or more of the soffit is beadboard, count the whole soffit as beadboard and write a Note that this is a local rule.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Canopy and porch counted again inside the eave or rake.
  • Not all eave runs traced (271 LFT instead of 310).
  • Rake and returns merged into the eave although the rows are different.
  • Truss heel hidden in the soffit SQ FT.
  • Soffit Eve Vinyl entered as framing instead of as material SQ FT.
  • 2x4 frame for soffit filled in automatically although the detail calls for 2x6.
  • For a roof of AJS Rafters with an open overhang, a simple rake counted instead of rafters by hand.

All roof mistakes: common-mistakes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Takeoffs/Main/eves rakes/eves/
  eve 24 main          Line  310 LFT
  eve 12 porch         Line   38 LFT
Takeoffs/Main/eves rakes/rakes/
  rake 12 main         Line   96 LFT
  returns 12           Line    8 LFT

Soffits at Eves      12" Vinyl vented    620   SQ FT   310 x 2'
Fascia at Eves       1x8 alum wrapped    341   LFT
One eave line gives several rows: soffit by area, fascia and sub fascia by length, overhang framing per detail.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Rake, Returns, Truss Heel
  • Soffit and Fascia - materials and LFT vs SQ FT
  • Roof Sheathing, Canopy, Porch SQFT

docs.title: Flashing (roof, walls, deck)
docs.text: Roof-to-wall intersection: step flashing stepped under the siding, kick-out at the bottom. Step flashing is counted in LFT along the intersection, kick-outs by the piece. Bottom of a roof-to-wall intersection: the last step of the step flashing turns into a kick-out that sends the water over the siding into the gutter. Step flashing is counted in LFT along the intersection line, one kick-out for each lower end of such a line. Photo: finehomebuilding.com, source, found via Pinterest.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Flashing is metal or tape at joints where water can get under the material: roof-to-wall intersections (step, kick-out), parapets (cap, coping, drip edge), horizontal wall joints (band, water table), deck or balcony-to-wall connections. Flashing around windows and doors is a separate page, Window Flashing: it has different rows and is split by wall type.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Architectural sections and details (sec, d) Rake, eave, parapet, cap flashing, step and kick-out; they are not on the structural sheets Wall sections Band flashing, water table, flashing over a build-out Roof plan (a105 rf) Roof-to-wall intersections, chimneys, valleys under metal Deck / balcony details Flashing along the ledger and under the decking Parapet details Coping or drip edge on top

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
1. Line tool along the joint: roof-to-wall intersection, top of the parapet, balcony ledger. LFT unit. Kick-outs are a Count of points.
  2. Name = product and location: step flashing, drip edge prpt, ledger flashing blcny. Folder per the job's agreed tree (roof misc or trims).
  3. Parapet: the parapet top length from parapets/prpt ...; coping on a separate row or in Drip Edge per detail.
  4. Roof, wall and deck flashing are counted independently of opening flashing: they are different rows.

To be confirmed

There is no single branch for flashing in the tree; confirmed takeoff names exist only for windows (Window Flashing). Keep flashing in one folder per job.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row
docs.text: Takeoff name DFL row Material Unit roof misc/step flashing Flashings at Wall step flashing, kick-out pcs LFT, pcs parapets/prpt 3.4 3 2 par Flashing Drip Edge / coping LFT sqfts/rf mtl 4 (valleys) Ice and Water (eves&valleys) per spec SQ FT / LFT framing/blcny/details/ledger flashing Head Trim Flashing / Flashing(s) per detail LFT

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Kick-outs and step flashing at roof-to-wall intersections forgotten.
  • Parapet flashing and coping counted twice (Flashing row and Drip Edge).
  • Flashing looked for only on the structural sheets.
  • Roof flashing mixed into the Window Flashing rows.

All roof mistakes: common-mistakes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Flashing             Drip Edge            186   LFT   parapet top, 5/A501
Flashings at Wall    Step flashing         64   LFT   roof to wall, 7/A502
Kick-out             pcs                    4   pcs

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Window Flashing, Exterior Wall Materials
  • Parapet, Eve / Eave, Rake

docs.title: Rake
docs.text: The rake is the sloped roof edge along the gable slope; the eave is the horizontal bottom edge. Two different lines, two different folders.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The rake is the sloped roof edge on the gable side, where the roof overhangs the gable. It differs from the eave in direction (along the slope, not horizontal), framing (lookouts/outriggers instead of truss tails) and its set of rows. The canon for the whole eave, including units and soffit, is on the Eve / Eave page.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof plan (a105 rf) Sloped edges at the gables, overhang Elevations (el) Rake fascia, barge board, trim, FRT on exposed wood Details (d) Lookouts 2x4/2x6, frame for rakes, sub fascia

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
1. Line tool along the sloped edge on the roof plan. LFT unit.
  2. Name rake <overhang in inches> <zone>: rake 12 main, rake 24 main. The eves rakes/rakes folder is created from the name automatically.
  3. The length on the plan is the plan length. Decide once whether you need the true sloped length (via the pitch); do not apply the pitch a second time.
  4. Canopy and porch are not part of the rake. Returns are their own takeoff (Returns).
  5. A roof of AJS Rafters with an open overhang: count the rafters by hand as framing, not as a simple rake.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row
docs.text: Takeoff name DFL row Material Unit eves rakes/rakes/rake 12 main Soffits at Rakes 9" Vinyl / beadboard LFT or SQ FT same line Fascia at Rakes 1x8 / alum wrapped LFT same line Frame for Rakes 24" o.c. 2x4 per detail LFT same line Sub Fascia 2x8 LFT

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Rake merged with the eave into one line.
  • Pitch applied both in the takeoff and in the formula.
  • Canopy or porch counted again in the rake.
  • FRT on an exposed rake not checked against the exterior wall rules.

All roof mistakes: common-mistakes.

docs.text:
Takeoffs/Main/eves rakes/rakes/

Takeoffs/Grge/eves rakes/rakes/

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: A return is the short piece of eave that turns onto the gable and dies into the rake. A separate takeoff, a separate set of trim.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A return (eave return, cornice return) is the box at the gable corner where the horizontal eave turns into the sloped rake. Two kinds: a proper cornice return (soffit + fascia + crown) and a pork-chop (a simple triangular stub, but it still has fascia and a small soffit). A return is part of neither the eave nor the rake: different framing and a different set of rows.

Pork-chop return: a triangle, we count fascia and soffit Cornice return: soffit, fascia, crown as a separate set

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text:
Sheet What to take Elevations (el) Whether there are returns, how many corners, type Architectural details (d) Pork-chop or cornice; return length, trim Roof plan (a105 rf) Where the eave meets the rake

Returns are not shown on the structural sheets: open the elevations and details.

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
1. Line tool along the short return piece along the gable wall, on the roof plan or elevation. LFT unit.
  2. Name returns <overhang in inches>: returns 12. Folder eves rakes/rakes or eves per the job's agreed tree; a name with returns is routed like a rake.
  3. One return = one segment; the number of corners shows in the number of takeoffs.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row
docs.text: Takeoff name DFL row Material Unit eves rakes/rakes/returns 12 Rafter Frame for returns 2x4 per detail LFT same line Soffits at Eves (part) / Fascia per detail SQ FT / LFT cornice Crown at returns per detail LFT

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Returns dissolved into the overall eave line.
  • Type not determined (pork-chop vs cornice): different trim and SQ FT.
  • FRT for exposed wood not checked.

All roof mistakes: common-mistakes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Takeoffs/Main/eves rakes/rakes/
  returns 12      Line  8 LFT   (4 corners at 2')

docs.title: See also

docs.title: Ridge / Valley / Hip
docs.text: Ridge is the top line, hip is the outside sloped edge, valley is the inside one. On the roof plan these are three different line types.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
• Ridge: the horizontal line where two slopes meet at the top.
  • Hip: the sloped outside edge, the slopes meet at a convex corner.
  • Valley: the sloped inside edge, the slopes meet at a concave corner.

On a truss roof all three lines are part of the trusses by others; we count only what is shown loose: ridge board between gable trusses, overframe valley sleepers, flashing. On a stick roof the ridge beam, hip and valley rafters are our framing. Details for each element: Ridge, Hip, Valley.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Roof framing plan (S) Trusses or rafters; size of the ridge beam, hip and valley rafters, LVL/PSL Arch roof plan (a105 rf) Ridge, hip, valley lines; lengths; overframes Details (d) Ridge beam bearing, posts under the ridge, valley sleepers, metal valley

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
1. Ridge beam: Beam tool along the span between supports, takeoff in framing/roof framing/beams/<size> <length> (for example (2) 1 3/4 x 11 7/8 LVL 22); the tool rounds the length itself.
  2. Hip and valley rafters: Line along the edge line on the plan, in framing/roof framing/details/<size> hip or the job's agreed branch; plan length, pitch applied once in the formula.
  3. Ridge board between trusses and overframe sleepers: Line in details.
  4. Metal valley flashing: Flashing, if in scope.

To be confirmed

There is no fixed single branch for hip and valley rafters in the tree; on each job keep them in one roof framing folder, not in sqfts.

docs.title: Takeoff name and DFL row
docs.text: Takeoff name DFL row Material Unit framing/roof framing/beams/(2) 1 3/4 x 11 7/8 LVL 22 Ridge (2) LVL pcs + length framing/roof framing/details/2x12 hip Hip plates / rafter per template 2x12 LFT framing/roof framing/details/2x12 valley Ridge / Valley / Hip 2x12 LFT

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Hip and valley rafters taken as common rafters: they are longer and bigger.
  • Ridge beam on a truss roof counted as ours although the trusses are by others.
  • Pitch applied twice (in the takeoff and in the formula).
  • Framing and roof trim along the same lines merged into one row.

All roof mistakes: common-mistakes.

docs.title: Roof Types
docs.text: Flat roof: membrane, cover board, rigid insulation, deck. All layers over the same area, each on its own row.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: The roof type sets which area materials go into the DFL on top of the framing: pitched under shingles, pitched under metal, flat under a membrane, canopy and small roofs. The framing (trusses, rafters) is covered on the Roof Framing pages, the deck on Roof Sheathing. This page is about not losing a layer that only this type has.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Arch roof plan (a105 rf) Zones by type: shingles, metal, flat, canopy; pitches Roof assemblies (ft), specs Flat roof layers: cover board, rigid, tapered, XPS, EPDM; alternates Sections (sec) Canopy and stair lid: second deck layer, tapered, DensGlass underneath Structural notes Deck for each type: 19/32", 1/2" Ply under metal, 3/4" flat

docs.title: Types and their rows
docs.text:
Type Takeoff name What it brings into the DFL Unit Pitched under shingles sqfts/rf 6 Roof Sheathing, Clips, Felt for Roof, Ice and Water (eves&valleys) if in scope 4x8, pcs, SQ FT Pitched under metal sqfts/rf mtl 4 Roof Sheathing (metal) 1/2" Ply; the metal itself is by others, Metal Roofs only if in scope 4x8 Overframe sqfts/overframe 4 Roof Sheathing (overframes), sleepers per detail 4x8, LFT Flat sqfts/flat, sqfts/ply flat Roof Sheathing at Flat Roofs 3/4", Densdeck / cover board, Rigid Insulation, XPS, EPDM at flat roofs 4x8, SQ FT Canopy, upper porch sqfts/flat canopy or per the canopy block 3/4" T&G, tapered insulation, 5/8" Ext Gyp or DensGlass underneath (two soffit rows) 4x8, SQ FT Stair lid, mech screen its own Area two deck layers (1/2" Ply + 3/4" OSB), kickers per detail 4x8

Each type has its own outline and its own pitch; the pitch of the neighboring roof is not inherited. Alternates (shingles and standing seam on the same plan): state in a Note what was counted, or count both as alternates.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• On a flat roof, Densdeck / cover board and the second XPS layer over the same area missed.
  • Canopy counted as a piece of the main roof, without tapered insulation and without the gypsum underneath.
  • Piggyback trusses without sleepers.
  • Metal by others, but the ply under it not counted.
  • Shingles and metal on the same plan, one chosen without a Note.

All roof mistakes: common-mistakes.

docs.text:
Takeoffs/Main/sqfts/
  rf 6          Area  5880 SF   (main, shingles)
  rf mtl 4      Area   410 SF   (porch roof, standing seam)
  flat          Area   960 SF   (flat section, EPDM)
Takeoffs/Grge/sqfts/
  rf 4          Area  1420 SF

docs.title: EIFS / Stucco / Veneer
docs.text: Finish systems by others. WRB, sheathing, furring and wood/PVC trim around them are ours. J-channel is ours only with vinyl siding. EIFS in progress: EPS boards on washer-head fasteners, fiberglass mesh on top, embedded in the base coat. All of it is by others; our rows are the sheathing and WRB under the boards and the trim at the edges. Photo: estimatingedge.com, source, found via Pinterest. Three-coat stucco: the first coat (scratch coat) with grooves over metal lath, windows taped off. Stucco is by others; our scope under it is sheathing, WRB and wood trim at the openings. Photo: hometips.com, source, found via Pinterest. Adhered stone veneer: metal lath visible at the top, scratch coat below, stone set in mortar on it. The whole package is by others; under it are our sheathing and WRB, wood trim at the edges. Photo: mountainviewstone.net, source, found via Pinterest.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: EIFS, stucco, stone veneer and brick veneer are also exterior wall cladding, but they are separate trades. In our scope (wood, EWP, vinyl, fiber cement and trim) the finish itself is not counted. We count what is under it and around it: WRB, sheathing, furring, wood/PVC trim, soffit, fascia.

docs.title: How to recognize it on the plans
docs.text:
EIFSStuccoStone veneerBrick veneer

Exterior Insulation and Finish System, "synthetic stucco": adhesive, insulation board (EPS), base coat with fiberglass mesh, finish coat. Notes EIFS, Synthetic Stucco, Dryvit, Sto, Senergy, 1" / 2" EIFS; in section, insulation board and thin layers with mesh; on the elevation, smooth fields with reveals and expansion joints. By others (EIFS sub).

Cement plaster, usually 3-coat (scratch, brown, finish) over metal lath and WRB. Notes Stucco, 3-coat stucco, Cement plaster, Portland; in section, lath and three coats, weep screed at the bottom. By others (plaster trade).

Cladding stone, manufactured or natural, adhered on a scratch coat or anchored. Notes Stone Veneer, Cultured Stone, Manufactured Stone; stone hatch on the elevation; in section, WRB, lath, scratch coat, stone. By others (mason).

Brick cladding with an air gap, brick ties to the frame, weep holes, lintels and shelf angles. Notes Brick Veneer, Brick, brick hatch; in section, air gap, ties, weeps. By others (mason).

docs.title: What we count next to it
docs.text:
Element Count it? WRB under the cladding (per spec) yes, check the scope Sheathing (CDX, OSB, Zip) yes, its own scope Furring and framing for the cladding yes, if shown Wood / PVC trim, corner, band, soffit, fascia yes The EIFS, stucco, stone, brick itself no Lath, base coat, brick ties, shelf angle, casing bead no, by others
  • A note is required: Note: Stone Veneer by others, Note: Stucco by others, Note: EIFS by others.
  • The whole elevation is EIFS, stucco or stone: siding 0 SQ FT plus a note, trim close to zero. Do not pad the quantity.
  • EIFS and stucco accessories (casing bead, stop bead, track, expansion joint) come with the system by others. J-channel with vinyl siding is ours; canonical page: Exclusions and J-Channel.

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text: No separate takeoff is needed for cladding by others. The wall area under it is needed for WRB and sheathing: it comes from walls and the wall height, not from the elevation. Trim around the cladding is counted as usual in trims.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Stone or brick veneer counted as siding or as our masonry.
  • WRB and sheathing under EIFS missed because "the wall is by others".
  • EIFS casing bead written as our J-channel.
  • The by-others note not added.
  • All sheathing and WRB mistakes: Sheathing.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Note: Stone Veneer and EIFS are by others; WRB and sheathing counted
Siding          Per plans: EIFS by others     0      SQ FT
WRB             fluid-applied per spec        6 420  SQ FT   A3.0
Wall Sheathing  7/16" Zip                     215    4x8     8/S3.0
CornerBoards    5/4x6 PVC                     112    LFT     A201

docs.text:
• Siding, Underlayment, Measuring
  • Exclusions and J-Channel, Casing, Corner & Band
  • Wall Sheathing, Standard notes

docs.title: Measuring siding
docs.text: SQ FT by elevation: the wall field is an Area, gable and accent as separate areas, large openings deducted once.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Siding is counted by area in SQ FT per elevation, wall by wall. Trim, accessories and flashing are counted separately in LFT and pcs; they are not part of the siding area.

docs.title: Where to find it on the plans
docs.text: Sheet What to take Elevations (el) Area of each elevation, material by zone, gables, bays, dormers Wall sections Wall height up to the soffit, flare, furring Plans and opening layout Large openings to deduct (overhead doors, storefronts) Notes by others, TBD, product

docs.title: How to measure in OurPlanCore
docs.text:
1. Open the elevation sheet. Elevations have no sheet dot, so the item is created in the siding root manually or by a name rule.
  2. Area along the wall field of each elevation: one item per material and color (6" vertical, panel grey, shingle gable). One material on several elevations can be collected as several polygons in one item.
  3. Gables, dormers, bays, return walls as separate polygons or items, especially with a different material.
  4. Cut large openings out as holes in the Area; windows under 4' are not deducted, they go to waste. Do not deduct the same opening twice (siding and WRB each take the deduction from their own area).
  5. Check the elevation scale against a known dimension (floor height, overhead door width): elevations are often at a different scale than the plans.
  6. Move the area to the DFL with a formula with visible addends and update it after the takeoff is edited.

docs.title: Tree name and DFL row
docs.text:
Tree name DFL row Unit Formula siding/6" vertical Siding Vertical 1x6 Cedar SQ FT =Front+Rear+Left+Right siding/panel grey Siding Fiber Cement Panel grey SQ FT separately by color siding/shingle gable Siding Gable front Vinyl Shingles SQ FT accent separately Siding (correction) SQ FT -140 as a visible row, if a deduction is needed Siding Per customer TBD SQ FT 0 plus a note

Waste: lap is moderate, shingle and shake higher, diagonal and small gables give more offcuts. Keep the factor as a visible multiplier per Formulas and factors.

docs.title: By others and TBD
docs.text:
• Siding by others: a row with 0 and the note by others or by customer.
  • Material not specified: Per customer TBD or verify material, do not substitute a product.
  • EIFS, stucco, stone, brick: not counted, but check the WRB, sheathing, furring and trim next to them: EIFS / Stucco / Veneer.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Area from the plan (perimeter x height) without deducting gables and without the different wall heights per elevation.
  • An opening deducted twice or not at all (garage doors).
  • Elevation scale not checked.
  • Area measured but not moved to Excel or not updated.
  • All area and sheathing mistakes: SQFT areas, Sheathing.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Takeoffs/Main/siding/6" vertical     Area   4 polygons   3 180 SF
Takeoffs/Main/siding/shingle gable   Area   2 polygons     420 SF

Siding Vertical      1x6 Cedar              3 180  SQ FT   =1120+940+560+560   A201 A202
Siding Gable front   Cedar Shingles 5-1/2"    420  SQ FT   =210+210            A201
